title: Chalmers puts super at forefront of next election
full_text:
Superannuation will be “front and centre” of Australia’s economy and “crucial” to making the future work for the country, Treasurer Jim Chalmers has said.
In a speech to the Super Members Council Super Summit, held on 9 September, Chalmers gave a glimpse of the latest Intergenerational Report (IGR) findings and said super is a “broader antidote” to the serious intergenerational pressures facing Australia.
Chalmers bought forward the release of the latest report in response to the One Nation super proposal released on 7 September which would allow people paying rent or a mortgage to divert one quarter of their future super contributions into their take-home pay for up to three years.
Under the One Nation proposal, those paying rent or a mortgage on the home they live in can choose to receive one quarter of their future compulsory super contributions as tax advantaged take-home pay for up to three years. Existing super cannot be touched and the scheme would not apply to investment properties.
Those who choose to take part will be required to establish eligibility directly with their super fund using evidence such as a lease, rental statement or mortgage statement.
The One Nation plan states that employers of those who take up the option would keep paying the full 12 per cent compulsory super contribution, with nine per cent remaining in super for retirement and three per cent paid directly to the participant by their super fund.
The policy only applies to future contributions. The three per cent portion allocated to participants will keep the concessional tax treatment which means it will be taxed at 15 per cent rather than their higher personal income-tax rate.
One Nation estimates a full-time worker earning about $90,500 could receive around $2,300 a year, or $44 a week, in additional take-home income.
The Treasurer said new Treasury projections indicate the number of Australians over Age Pension age will almost double to around nine million by 2066, but the IGR analysis shows the share of older Australians receiving a pension or income support payment is expected to fall, from 66 per cent last year to 52 per cent by 2066.
“This means spending on Age and service pensions is projected to fall from 2.3 per cent of GDP last year to 1.8 per cent in 2066.In comparison, that number is nearly 10 per cent by 2060 in the UK, eight per cent in Canada, seven per cent in New Zealand, and six per cent in the US,” he said.
“If Age Pension expenditure in Australia was still at 2.3 per cent in 2065–66, the annual bill would be $31 billion higher in today’s dollars. Super takes serious pressure off social security outlays and makes the budget much more sustainable as a consequence.”
He continued that the median retirement age balance is set to approach $450,000 over the next decade.
“That’s a big leap from a bit over $200,000 in the latest data – another considerable improvement on the $115,000 a decade earlier. And drawdowns from superannuation are projected to double to around six per cent of GDP by 2066,” he said.
“The $4 trillion super pool is also a key driver of the growth in foreign income inflows, supporting our gross national income. So, while it’s boosting retirement incomes it’s helping to unlock investment here and abroad, reduce reliance on the pension, strengthen international relationships and deepen our capital markets.”
Chalmers said the Government is now in the middle of the next set of reforms to ensure super is working in members’ best interests including the reforms on consumer protection advice and compensation announced by Financial Services Minister Daniel Mulino last month, as well as consultation on the Performance Test.
“There’s a lot more work going into the retirement phase as well. We’re taking steps to ensure the retirement phase of super delivers more for members,” he said.
“Soon we’ll open up consultation on the innovative income streams regulations so funds can offer product features like money back guarantees and purchasing in instalments and provide fairer treatment for couples.”
Chalmers said presently people are not using their super to its full capacity and as super balances in retirement continue to grow, it will become even more important that retirees are supported to draw on their superannuation savings in retirement with more confidence.
“We’re witnessing now the biggest threat to compulsory super, with preservation at its core, in the four decades since it began. The crazy announcement by One Nation and the supportive comments from parts of the Coalition have made this very clear,” he said.
“They will end super as we know it and millions of workers will be poorer as a consequence. The next election will be super’s existential moment. It will help determine whether we make the most of our intergenerational advantages or trash them.”
author: Keeli Cambourne
